threats.title: [F-006] OAuth password derived from email — oauth.component.ts:30
threats.description:
An attacker who knows the email of a Google-OAuth-registered user computes btoa(reversed email), submits it with that email to the normal login form, and receives the victim's session token because the SPA registered the account with exactly that password.

Impact: Full account takeover of every OAuth-created account, including access to its orders, addresses, payment data, and basket in the training shop.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1391
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
oauth.component.ts:30 sets password = btoa(profile.email reversed) and saves the user with it at :31; login at :46 authenticates with the same derived value, so the credential is a deterministic function of the public email.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: e82578626535215a73f2dd4b284b623fade7af7fd4e0618023e74f0bb85c5c85

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-006 (F-006)
threats.mitigation:
M-107 — Remove email-derived password from OAuth registration (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Stop creating OAuth accounts with a client-computed password; send the Google access token (or an authorization code) to the server and have the server verify it with Google, then create the user with an unusable random password and issue the session.
2. Remove the btoa(reverse(email)) computation at oauth.component.ts:30 and :46 and drop password-based login for OAuth-flagged accounts on the server.
3. Add an API test that logging in via /rest/user/login with btoa(reversed email) for an OAuth-created user returns 401.
Verification: Create a user through the OAuth flow, then POST /rest/user/login with {email, password: btoa(email reversed)}; expect HTTP 401 instead of a token.
Reference: CWE-1391

threats.title: [F-022] JWT session token stored in localStorage — login.component.ts:101
threats.description:
An attacker who gets any script running in the shop origin (for example through the XSS sinks in this SPA) reads localStorage.token or the script-written token cookie and replays it as a Bearer token to act as the victim.

Impact: Any same-origin script can exfiltrate the session JWT, the declared sensitive asset, turning every XSS into full session hijack for its token lifetime.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-922
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:101 writes authentication.token to localStorage and :104 writes it to a cookie via cookieService.put (script-set, so it cannot be HttpOnly); oauth.component.ts:50-51 does the same; request.interceptor.ts:16 reads it back for every request; login.component.ts:120 also stores the 2FA tmpToken in localStorage.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: e82578626535215a73f2dd4b284b623fade7af7fd4e0618023e74f0bb85c5c85

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-022 (F-022)
threats.mitigation:
M-117 — Store session tokens in HttpOnly, Secure cookies (F-022) (priority P3, effort High)
1. Have the login endpoint set the session as an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie and stop returning the raw token to the SPA; remove localStorage.setItem('token') at login.component.ts:101 and oauth.component.ts:51 and the cookieService.put calls.
2. Replace the Authorization header in request.interceptor.ts with cookie-based auth plus a CSRF token, and keep the 2FA tmpToken in memory rather than localStorage.
3. Add an E2E check that after login localStorage has no 'token' key and document.cookie does not contain the session token.
Verification: After login in Cypress, assert window.localStorage.getItem('token') is null and document.cookie does not include 'token='; expect both to pass.
Reference: CWE-922

threats.title: [F-035] OAuth implicit flow without state check — oauth.component.ts:28
threats.description:
An attacker sends a victim a link to the shop ending in #access_token=<attacker Google token>; the oauth route matches any fragment containing access_token, the SPA logs the victim into the attacker's shop account, and payment cards or addresses the victim enters land in the attacker's account.

Impact: Login CSRF: the victim unknowingly acts inside an attacker-controlled account, exposing data they enter (addresses, cards, complaints) to the attacker.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-352
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:148 starts the flow with response_type=token and no state or nonce; app.routing.ts:286 routes any URL containing #access_token= to OAuthComponent, and oauth.component.ts:28 consumes the fragment token without comparing any stored state.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:28

threats.mitigation:
M-128 — Add anti-CSRF protection to state-changing requests (F-035) (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Switch googleLogin() at login.component.ts:148 to response_type=code with a PKCE S256 challenge and a random state stored in sessionStorage.

Impact: One message blocks the event loop for an extrapolated tens of minutes at 1 MB, making every HTTP and socket endpoint of the application unavailable; repeated messages sustain the outage.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1333
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 46 runs /.*\.\.\/\.\.\/\.\.[\w/-]*?\/redirect.../ via data?.match on raw client data with no length check; the Server at line 20 sets no maxHttpBufferSize. A local node run measured 49 ms at 5,000 chars, 165 ms at 10,000 and 829 ms at 20,000, confirming quadratic growth.

The server registers a 'verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge' WebSocket event that checks only Array.isArray(data) && data.length > 1; any unauthenticated socket can emit this event with a trivial payload (e.g. [1,2]) to trigger challengeUtils.solveIf and mark the challenge solved. No authentication or session check is applied to any WebSocket event handler. The exclusion (server-side verification of challenge state) is absent: the server validates only payload shape, not whether the user actually dismissed multiple notifications. Other verify events (verifyLocalXssChallenge, verifySvgInjectionChallenge) require knowledge of specific payloads and are harder to abuse; the closeNotifications case has no such protection.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-306
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-087 (F-087)
threats.mitigation:
M-167 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (F-087) (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Authenticate WebSocket connections and verify challenge state server-side before crediting…
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the security scan; the CWE-306 finding at lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50 is cleared, and the regression test passes.

data.name: Web3 / Wallet / NFT Surface
data.description: Handles Ethereum Sepolia blockchain interactions: NFT minting via wallet address verification, crypto-key submission challenges, and exploit-address challenges. Uses ethers.js with Alchemy RPC at eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com. Includes an open redirect handler.

threats.title: [F-031] Hardcoded BIP39 wallet mnemonic in source — routes/checkKeys.ts:10
threats.description:
An attacker reads the public repository or the shipped server bundle, copies the 12-word mnemonic literal, derives the private key with any BIP39 wallet and takes full control of the Ethereum wallet, then submits that key to /rest/web3/submitKey.

Impact: Anyone with source access controls the wallet derived from the mnemonic (any funds or tokens on it) and can solve the key-submission check without discovering the key; the secret cannot be rotated without a code change.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/checkKeys.ts:10 assigns a literal 12-word BIP39 mnemonic, and line 11 derives the HD wallet and private key from it at runtime, so the reusable secret ships in version control and every deployment.
- routes/checkKeys.ts:10

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-005 [inconclusive, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-031 (F-031)
threats.mitigation:
M-125 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Delete the mnemonic literal; store only a keccak256 hash of the expected private key (or load the key from a secret store via environment) and compare req.body.privateKey against it in constant time.
2. Add a secret-scanning check (e.g. gitleaks with a BIP39 rule) in CI and a unit test asserting checkKeys.ts contains no mnemonic literal.
Verification: grep -nE "'([a-z]+ ){11}[a-z]+'" routes/checkKeys.ts returns no match and gitleaks detect exits 0.
Reference: CWE-798

threats.title: [F-068] Unbounded wallet Set growth from anonymous POSTs — routes/web3Wallet.ts:16
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker scripts many POSTs to /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress, each with a large unique walletAddress string; every value is added to the process-wide walletsConnected Set and is only removed when a matching on-chain ContractExploited event arrives, so heap usage grows until the Node process slows or crashes.

Impact: Sustained requests exhaust server memory and degrade or crash the shared Express process, taking down every other shop function.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-770
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/web3Wallet.ts:15-16 adds req.body.walletAddress to a module-level Set before any validation, with no type/length check, size cap, eviction, authentication or rate limit (server.ts:645 registers the route without middleware).
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-068 (F-068)
threats.mitigation:
M-158 — Validate and bound walletsConnected (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Accept walletAddress only when ethers.isAddress() passes, store the checksummed form, and cap walletsConnected (e.g. LRU of 1000 entries with TTL); add a rateLimit middleware on /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress.
2. Add an API test that posts a non-address value and expects 400, and a unit test asserting the Set size never exceeds the cap.
Verification: POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress with walletAddress='x'.repeat(50000) returns 400.
Reference: CWE-770

threats.title: [F-069] Leaked RPC WebSocket providers on error reset — routes/nftMint.ts:21
threats.description:
When the Alchemy RPC socket errors (for example ALCHEMY_API_KEY is unset or invalid), the onerror handler resets isEventListenerCreated without destroying the provider; an anonymous attacker then repeatedly calls GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen so each call opens another WebSocketProvider and contract listener that is never closed.

Impact: Accumulating sockets, timers and listeners exhaust file descriptors and memory in the shared server process and generate outbound connection floods against the RPC provider, which can also burn the Alchemy API quota.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-772
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/nftMint.ts:18 creates a new WebSocketProvider per call while the flag is false and line 21 sets isEventListenerCreated=false on error without provider.destroy(); routes/web3Wallet.ts:20-23 repeats the pattern; neither route has authentication or rate limiting (server.ts:643, 645).
- routes/nftMint.ts:21

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-069 (F-069)
threats.mitigation:
M-159 — Destroy failed providers and serialize listener creation in nftMint.ts and web3Wallet.ts (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Keep the provider in a module variable, call provider.destroy() in the onerror handler before clearing the flag, and create at most one provider at a time (guard with an in-flight promise and backoff); skip listener creation when ALCHEMY_API_KEY is absent.
2. Add a unit test that triggers onerror and calls the handler repeatedly, asserting only one live provider exists and destroy() was called.
Verification: With ALCHEMY_API_KEY unset, 100 GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen calls leave at most one open WebSocket (ss -tp shows a single connection to eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com).
Reference: CWE-772

data.name: CI/CD Pipeline
data.description: GitHub Actions pipeline with 16 workflows covering CI, CodeQL SAST, ZAP DAST, release packaging, Docker image publication, and frontend bundle analysis. ci.yml has no top-level permissions block; postinstall executes npm install and frontend build at dependency install time.

threats.title: [F-016] Lockfile disabled for npm installs
threats.description:
An attacker who publishes a malicious version of any transitive dependency within a declared semver range has it resolved fresh by every CI `npm install` (ci.yml:51, ci.yml:238) and by the image build (Dockerfile:5), because .npmrc disables lockfile generation and package-lock.json is gitignored.

Impact: A poisoned dependency ships inside the published Docker image and release archives and executes in every downstream deployment, with no lockfile diff to reveal the change.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
.npmrc:1 and frontend/.npmrc:1 set package-lock=false, .gitignore:10 ignores package-lock.json, and no lockfile is tracked in git; CI and Dockerfile use `npm install`, not `npm ci`. Global CLI installs (ci.yml:236 @angular/cli, release.yml:40 grunt-cli) are also unversioned.
- .npmrc:1

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-5 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): The npm registry to CI install crossing assumes lockfile-resolved installs; package-lock=false makes every install resolve fresh from the registry.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-016 (F-016)
threats.mitigation:
M-115 — Commit lockfiles and install from them (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove package-lock=false from .npmrc and frontend/.npmrc, drop package-lock.json from both .gitignore files, commit the generated lockfiles, and replace `npm install` with `npm ci` in ci.yml, release.yml, and Dockerfile:5; pin global CLI tools to exact versions.
2. Add a CI step that fails when `npm ci` reports a lockfile/manifest mismatch.
Verification: Run `git ls-files | grep -c package-lock.json` (expect 2) and `grep -rn 'npm install' .github/workflows Dockerfile` (expect no unpinned dependency installs).
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-038] Unsigned published container image
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the long-lived DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (release.yml:77) pushes a backdoored bkimminich/juice-shop tag; because the pipeline neither signs images nor publishes a verifiable signature, downstream users cannot distinguish the forged image from one built by this pipeline.

Impact: Users who pull the public image run attacker-controlled code on their training hosts with no cryptographic way to detect publisher impersonation.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
release.yml:86 and ci.yml:338 push multi-arch images with docker/build-push-action using username/password login; no cosign, sigstore, or attestation step exists in any workflow (zero-hit search).
- .github/workflows/release.yml:86

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-11 ci-cd-pipeline → external (outbound): The image push crossing to Docker Hub carries no signature, so consumers cannot verify that only pipeline-built images were published.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-038 (F-038)
threats.mitigation:
M-131 — Sign and verify release artifacts (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add id-token: write to the docker jobs, run sigstore/cosign-installer pinned by SHA, and keyless-sign the pushed digest from docker/build-push-action outputs.digest; add actions/attest-build-provenance for the same digest.
2. Document `cosign verify` with the GitHub OIDC issuer and workflow identity in the README and add a post-push CI step that runs the verification.
Verification: Run `cosign verify bkimminich/juice-shop:<tag> --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop/.github/workflows/release.yml@.*' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`; expect exit code 0 for pipeline images and failure for a manually pushed image.
Reference: CWE-345

threats.title: [F-045] Install script piped to shell unverified — ci.yml:358
threats.description:
An attacker who controls the content served at cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh gets arbitrary code executed in the heroku job, which then invokes the installed CLI with HEROKU_API_KEY to deploy master to the production juice-shop app.

Impact: A tampered installer can replace the heroku binary, capture the Heroku API key, and alter the deployed public demo instances.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-494
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:358 runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no checksum or signature check (zero hits for sha256sum/shasum/gpg in ci.yml); ci.yml:371 passes secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY to the deploy step in the same job.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-6 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): The remote install script crossing assumes integrity verification before execution; the script is piped straight to sh.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-045 (F-045)
threats.mitigation:
M-138 — Install the Heroku CLI from a pinned, checksum-verified artifact (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace the curl|sh step with `npm install -g heroku@<exact version>` or download a versioned tarball and verify it with `sha256sum -c` against a committed checksum before extraction.
2. Fail the job when the checksum does not match.
Verification: Run `grep -nE 'curl[^|]*\|\s*(ba)?sh' .github/workflows/*.yml`; expect no output.
Reference: CWE-494

threats.title: [F-046] Untrusted npm Install/Postinstall Scripts Enabled
threats.description:
Dependency Install Scripts Run at Build Time: Without --ignore-scripts, any compromised dependency publisher can execute postinstall code at build time.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-506
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- Dockerfile:4

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-046 (F-046)
threats.mitigation:
M-090 — Use npm ci --ignore-scripts in Dockerfile and audit required postinstalls (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace `npm install --omit=dev` in Dockerfile with `npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts`; switch any global install (`npm install -g`) to pin an exact version and add `--ignore-scripts`.
2. Audit package.json and its dependency tree for genuinely required install-time scripts (e.g., native addon compilation); run those explicitly with `npm run <script>` after install instead of relying on automatic hook execution.
3. Add a CI check that fails when any Dockerfile or workflow step running `npm install` or `npm ci` lacks `--ignore-scripts`.
Verification: Run `grep -nE 'npm (install|ci)' Dockerfile | grep -v -- '--ignore-scripts'`; expect no output.

threats.title: [F-047] Action pinned to mutable branch
threats.description:
An attacker who gains push access to calibreapp/image-actions commits malicious code to its main branch; the next image-change push to master or develop runs it with the repository GITHUB_TOKEN passed as githubToken.

Impact: Third-party code chosen by another repository's owner runs with a token that can write contents and pull requests, allowing commits or workflow changes in juice-shop.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
image_actions.yml:33 uses calibreapp/image-actions@main and passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN at line 35; lines 30 and 42 use tag refs @v6 and @v8. ci.yml:188 passes GITHUB_TOKEN to coverallsapp/github-action@v2 and codeql-analysis.yml:23 uses github/codeql-action/init@v3.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): The external GitHub Actions crossing assumes every action is SHA-pinned; this reference resolves a mutable branch at run time.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-047 (F-047)
threats.mitigation:
M-139 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (F-047) (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace calibreapp/image-actions@main, actions/checkout@v6, peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8, coverallsapp/github-action@v2, and github/codeql-action/*@v3 with full 40-character commit SHAs plus a version comment.
2. Add a CI lint (e.g. zizmor or a grep check) that fails on any `uses:` reference not matching @[0-9a-f]{40}.
Verification: Run `grep -nE 'uses: [^ ]+@' .github/workflows/*.yml | grep -vE '@[0-9a-f]{40}'`; expect no output.
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-048] Base image pulled by mutable tag
threats.description:
An attacker who replaces the gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 or node:24 tag content gets that layer built into every bkimminich/juice-shop image the docker jobs push, because the Dockerfile references tags instead of digests.

Impact: A substituted runtime base layer would run inside every published Juice Shop container without any change in this repository.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Dockerfile:1 uses FROM node:24 and Dockerfile:22 uses FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 without @sha256 digests; test/smoke/Dockerfile:1 uses FROM alpine.
- Dockerfile:22

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-4 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): The base image pull crossing assumes a content-addressed digest; the runtime stage resolves a mutable tag at build time.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-048 (F-048)
threats.mitigation:
M-140 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:22 to `FROM <image>:<tag>@sha256:<digest>` and let Dependabot or Renovate update the digests.
2. Add a CI check that fails when a FROM line lacks @sha256.
Verification: Run `grep -nE '^FROM ' Dockerfile test/smoke/Dockerfile | grep -v '@sha256:'`; expect no output.
Reference: CWE-1357

threats.title: [F-059] Install scripts run before secret-bearing step — ci.yml:238
threats.description:
An attacker whose malicious npm package is resolved during `npm install` at ci.yml:238 uses its install hook to plant code in node_modules that the next step loads, reading CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY, ALCHEMY_API_KEY, E2E_SOLUTIONS_WEBHOOK, and GITHUB_TOKEN from the Cypress step environment (ci.yml:250-253).

Impact: Repository and third-party service credentials leave the runner, enabling Cypress dashboard abuse, Alchemy API quota theft, and GITHUB_TOKEN use during the job.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:238 runs `npm install` without --ignore-scripts, which also runs the root postinstall (package.json:56) that installs and builds the frontend; ci.yml:241-253 then starts the app from the same workspace with four secrets in the step env.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:238

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-059 (F-059)
threats.mitigation:
M-150 — Disable dependency install scripts in secret-bearing CI jobs (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Install with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in e2e-test and api-test jobs and run only the required first-party build scripts explicitly; keep secrets out of jobs that execute freshly resolved dependency code where possible.
2. Add a CI check that fails when a job referencing `secrets.` runs `npm install` or `npm ci` without --ignore-scripts.
Verification: Run `grep -nE 'npm (install|ci)( |$)' .github/workflows/ci.yml | grep -v -- '--ignore-scripts'`; expect no output for jobs that reference secrets.
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-071] Workflow lacks permissions block — ci.yml:25
threats.description:
An attacker who gets code running in any ci.yml job, for example through a poisoned dependency or the mutable coverallsapp/github-action@v2 reference, uses the inherited GITHUB_TOKEN; if the repository default token scope is read-write, the token can push commits, edit releases, or alter workflows.

Impact: A compromised CI step can gain repository write access beyond what lint, test, or coverage jobs need, turning a build-time compromise into source tampering.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml declares no top-level or job-level permissions key (zero hits), so every job inherits the repository default GITHUB_TOKEN scope; GITHUB_TOKEN is passed explicitly at ci.yml:190, 253, 268, and 389. image_actions.yml and rebase.yml also lack permissions blocks.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:25

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-071 (F-071)
threats.mitigation:
M-161 — Drop unnecessary privileges in build and runtime (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of ci.yml and grant job-level write scopes only where needed (e.g. image_actions build job: contents: write, pull-requests: write; rebase job: contents: write).
2. Set the repository default workflow permissions to read-only and add a workflow lint that fails when a workflow lacks a permissions key.
Verification: Run `for f in .github/workflows/*.yml; do grep -q '^permissions:' "$f" || echo "$f"; done`; expect no output.
Reference: CWE-250

threats.title: [F-072] Container Runs as Root — Dockerfile:1
threats.description:
Container Runs as Root: Containers running as root expand container-escape blast radius.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- test/smoke/Dockerfile:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-072 (F-072)
threats.mitigation:
M-092 — Add non-root USER instruction to test/smoke/Dockerfile (priority P3, effort Low)
1. In test/smoke/Dockerfile, add `RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app` before the CMD instruction, then add `USER app` immediately after.
2. Verify the smoke test passes by running `docker build -f test/smoke/Dockerfile -t juice-shop-smoke . && docker run --rm juice-shop-smoke` and confirming exit code 0.
Verification: Run `grep -nE '^(USER|RUN)' test/smoke/Dockerfile | grep -i 'user'`; expect a non-root USER entry; confirm `docker inspect` shows User is not empty, root, or 0.

threats.title: [F-073] Missing Workflow Permissions Block
threats.description:
Missing Workflow Permissions Block: Without an explicit permissions block at workflow or job level, the job inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-732
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:25

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-073 (F-073)
threats.mitigation:
M-093 — Add least-privilege permissions blocks to all workflows lacking them (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add `permissions: contents: read` at the workflow root of ci.yml, image_actions.yml, and rebase.yml to restrict GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only by default.
2. Grant elevated write scopes at job level only where required: image_actions build job needs `contents: write` and `pull-requests: write`; rebase job needs `contents: write`.
3. Set the repository default workflow permissions to read-only in GitHub Settings > Actions > General so new workflows start from a least-privilege baseline.
4. Add a CI lint step that runs `for f in .github/workflows/*.yml; do grep -q 'permissions:' "$f" || exit 1; done` and fails when any workflow file lacks a permissions block.
Verification: Run `for f in .github/workflows/*.yml; do grep -q 'permissions:' "$f" || echo "MISSING: $f"; done`; expect no output.
